title: Abba (Mark 14:32–52)
hookLine: he calls God by the family word, and a young man flees leaving his linen cloth

cards: Most of us have had one night we'd never want to live again. Waiting for a phone call. Sitting by a bed.
Today is that night for Jesus. They come to Gethsemane, an olive grove at the foot of the Mount of Olives; the name probably means oil press.

He tells most of the disciples to sit and wait, takes Peter, James and John further in, and Mark says he began to be terrified and deeply troubled. My soul is sorrowful even unto death, he tells them. Stay here and watch.
Then he goes a little further alone, and falls on the ground.

teach.h: ABBA: THE FAMILY WORD FOR FATHER.
REMOVE THIS CHALICE. NOT MY WILL.
teach.b: Face down in the dirt, he prays, in the Douay-Rheims: "Abba, Father, all things are possible to thee: remove this chalice from me; but not what I will, but what thou wilt."
Abba is Aramaic, the everyday word for father inside a family. Mark keeps the sound, then translates it. You'll sometimes hear that abba means daddy.
Scholars now say that's too cute: grown children called their fathers abba too. It's close, trusting, family speech, at the worst moment of his life. Second, the honesty.
He asks for the cup to pass; he doesn't pretend to want it. Then he hands the choice back: not my will, yours. Catholics see here both his true human fear and his free obedience.

teach.h: ASLEEP THREE TIMES. WATCH AND PRAY.
teach.b: Three times he comes back and finds them asleep, two days after his speech ended on one word: watch. "Watch ye, and pray that you enter not into temptation. The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh weak."
Fourth, the arrest. Judas arrives with a crowd carrying swords and clubs, and greets Jesus with a kiss. Someone draws a sword and cuts off the ear of the high priest's servant.

teach.h: A KISS, A SWORD, AND THEY ALL FLED.
teach.b: And then, Mark says, they all left him and fled.

teach.h: ABBA, FATHER, ALL THINGS ARE POSSIBLE TO THEE.
teach.b: One detail only Mark tells: a young man following, wearing only a linen cloth. They grab him, and he leaves the cloth in their hands and runs away naked. Nobody knows who he was.
An old guess says it was Mark himself, signing his Gospel. The sources don't say.

how: On Holy Thursday night many Catholic parishes keep watch before the Blessed Sacrament until midnight, remembering Jesus's prayer in Gethsemane, and the Agony in the Garden is the first Sorrowful Mystery of the rosary.

o: baby talk for daddy, used by toddlers
the everyday family word for father
a formal title for a rabbi or teacher

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.

s: abba is baby talk, like daddy
grown children called their fathers abba too. it's close, trusting family speech, not baby talk.
only Mark tells the story of the young man in the linen cloth
no other Gospel has it, and nobody knows who he was.
Mark says he was terrified and troubled, and he asks for the cup to pass.

games.q: you're Peter in the garden. Jesus asked you to stay awake and watch. it's late, you've had wine and a long day. what happens?
o: you go back to the city.
games.why: he finds them sleeping three times: "The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh weak."

practice: Bring to mind the thing you most wish would pass from you right now, and say honestly that you don't want it. If you pray, you can use Jesus's own two words, Abba, Father, slowly, on your breath, as many times as you need.
If you don't, think of the person whose voice feels most like home, and rest in that for a minute.

wordCard.voice: Abba. Aramaic for father, the word used inside a family. Jesus says it face down in Gethsemane, the night before he dies. Today's word.

orig.note: Aramaic abba, then the Greek for the father: Mark keeps the word and translates it.

carryVoice: Your line: abba, father. Fear and trust, in the same breath. See you tomorrow.
